chapters.title: Chapter 5: ESOPs from the Company’s Side

lessons.title: Case Study: ESOP Wealth Stories and Cautionary Tales from Indian Companies

children.text: One instrument. The same law, the same tax, the same mechanics you have spent four chapters learning. And outcomes ranging from generational wealth to nothing at all. This closing lesson looks at what actually happened to Indian employees who held ESOPs, and what separated the two groups.

body.text: Almost none of the difference came from how many options people were granted. It came from whether a buyer ever appeared, at what price, and whether the employee had planned for the possibility that one never would.

children.text: Case One: Infosys, and the Idea That Started It

Infosys ran employee stock option plans through the 1990s that reached well beyond senior management, and by the end of the decade hundreds of its employees had become crorepatis. For a generation of Indian professionals, this was proof that salaried people could build real wealth through ownership rather than only through savings.

Two features made it work, and both are easy to miss. The company listed, so the shares had a market and a price. And the grants were broad, so the wealth was not confined to a handful of executives. Every later Indian ESOP story is measured against those two conditions.
Case Two: Flipkart, the Serial Liquidity Provider
Flipkart is the clearest Indian example of a company treating employee liquidity as a recurring obligation rather than a one-off event.

events.title: The Walmart deal
events.description: Walmart purchased employee stock options reported at around $800 million, at $126 to $128 a unit, with current employees able to liquidate 50% of vested options on closing, then 25% after one year and 25% after two.

events.title: The PhonePe separation payout
events.description: About $700 million paid to current and former employees, reported at $43.67 per vested option, compensating ESOP holders for the value that left with PhonePe.

events.title: A $50 million buyback
events.description: Employees could sell up to 5% of vested options, benefiting roughly 7,000 to 7,500 people, while the company remained unlisted.

body.text: Notice what an employee joining Flipkart in 2016 could not have known, and what one joining in 2024 could: that this company has a demonstrated pattern of converting employee options into cash. A track record is the single most useful piece of information available about an unlisted employer, and it is public.

children.text: Case Three: Swiggy, the Listing Payday
When Swiggy listed on the NSE and BSE in November 2024, years of unlisted options acquired a daily market price.

stats.context: 23.1 crore options at the ₹390 upper price band, as of September 2024

stats.label: Expected crorepatis

children.text: The listing did what no buyback can: it created a continuous market. But even here, employees faced lock-ins, trading windows and a share price that moved after listing. A listing converts paper into a price. It does not guarantee that the price is one you like.
Case Four: Paytm, Where Listing Was Not Enough

Paytm listed in November 2021 at an issue price of ₹2,150 a share. It closed its first day at about ₹1,955, a discount of roughly 9% to the issue price, fell to around ₹1,271 by late November 2021, and was at about ₹467 by September 2022.

body.title: Paytm share price milestones after listing, as reported

children.text: That is a fall of roughly 78% from the issue price. For employees holding options with an exercise price set against pre-IPO valuations, the consequence was brutal and simple: the options went
underwater

markDefs.definition: An option whose exercise price is above the current share value, making it worth nothing to exercise.

body.title: Value an Underwater Grant
body.prompt: An employee holds 3,000 options with an exercise price of ₹1,800. The share is trading at ₹467. What is the intrinsic value of the grant?
body.explanation: Intrinsic value cannot be negative: nobody pays ₹1,800 for something worth ₹467. The grant is worth nothing unless the share recovers above the exercise price before the options expire. The employee loses nothing out of pocket, provided they never exercised.

children.text: The worse version: exercising first, falling after

The employees who were genuinely hurt were those who exercised at a high valuation and paid perquisite tax on it. Suppose someone exercised 2,000 options at a ₹500 exercise price when the fair market value was ₹2,000.

body.caption: Exercising near the top, selling after the fall

cells: Paid to exercise
Perquisite taxed as salary
Tax paid on that perquisite, at 31.2%
Sale proceeds later, at ₹600 a share
Capital loss booked
Net cash position
₹7,36,000 out of pocket

body.text: This employee is ₹7.36 lakh out of pocket on a grant that was taxed as though it had made them ₹30 lakh richer. The perquisite tax is not refunded when the price falls, and the resulting capital loss can only be set against capital gains under the rules, not against salary. Exercising at a peak is the most expensive mistake in this course.

body.title: What to do if your options are underwater

children.text: If you have not exercised, do nothing. That is the whole point of an option: you are not obliged to buy. Track the expiry date, and revisit only if the share recovers meaningfully above your exercise price.

If you have exercised and hold shares now worth less, the tax is already paid and cannot be recovered. What remains is a portfolio decision, not an ESOP decision: would you buy this share today at this price with fresh money? If not, holding purely to recover a loss is a sunk cost argument rather than an investment case.

Some companies respond to sustained falls by granting fresh options at the lower price, which restores incentive for employees who stay. It does nothing for tax already paid, but it is worth asking whether such a refresh is planned.
Case Five: Byju’s, and the Limits of a Headline Valuation
Byju’s was valued at a peak of about $22 billion in 2022, making it India’s most valuable startup. A series of investor
markdowns
followed, and by late 2024 the company had entered insolvency proceedings with its valuation reported as having collapsed to effectively nothing.

markDefs.definition: A reduction in the value an investor carries a holding at, which signals a fall in the company’s estimated worth.

children.text: For employees, the mechanics were exactly as this course described. The exercise price stayed fixed while the value of the shares fell beneath it, so options that had once looked like a fortune on paper became worthless. Nobody had done anything wrong. The valuation that made the grants look valuable was never a price at which employees could sell.

columns.label: The Flipkart employee
points: Multiple liquidity windows across several years
Able to convert part of the holding at each one
Diversified gradually rather than betting on one date
Cash in hand well before any listing

columns.label: The employee at a company that collapsed
points: A headline valuation, and no route to sell against it
No buyback, so no chance to take anything off the table
Possibly perquisite tax already paid on a value that evaporated

children.text: What Separated the Outcomes

cells: Infosys, 1990s
Broad grants at a listed company created many crorepatis
Breadth plus a real market is what turns ESOPs into wealth
Flipkart, 2018 to 2025
Three separate payouts over seven years
A liquidity track record is the best signal an unlisted employer can give
Swiggy, 2024
Listing gave thousands of employees a tradeable price
A listing creates a market, not a guaranteed gain
Paytm, 2021 onwards
Listed, then fell roughly 78% from issue price
Being listed does not make options valuable; the exercise price decides that
Byju’s, 2022 onwards
Peak valuation of about $22 billion, then collapse
A valuation you cannot sell into is not your wealth

body.title: Which Signal Matters Most?
body.question: You are choosing between two unlisted companies offering similar grants. Which single piece of information tells you most about what your ESOPs are likely to be worth?
options: The valuation at the most recent funding round
Whether the company has run liquidity events before, and when
The number of options in the offer
The size of the total ESOP pool
body.explanation: The last round valuation prices preference shares, not your ordinary shares, and option counts and pool sizes mean nothing without a denominator and a buyer. A demonstrated history of buybacks or secondary sales tells you the company treats employee liquidity as an obligation, which is the difference between the Flipkart experience and the alternative.

body.title: Putting the Whole Course to Work
body.scenario: Meghna has an offer from a Series C healthtech company in Mumbai: ₹24 lakh cash, down from her current ₹32 lakh, plus 15,000 options at a ₹40 exercise price. The last round priced shares at ₹520. The company is seven years old, DPIIT recognised, has about 3 crore fully diluted shares, has raised roughly ₹900 crore across rounds, and has never run a buyback. The exercise window on exit is 90 days.
body.prompt: Work through what she should calculate and ask, and what you would advise.
body.modelAnswer: Start with ownership: 15,000 options against 3 crore fully diluted shares is 0.05% of the company. At the last round price the headline intrinsic value is 15,000 × ₹480 = ₹72,00,000, but that price values preference shares, so her ordinary shares sit behind roughly ₹900 crore of invested capital in any exit waterfall. She is giving up ₹8 lakh a year, so ₹32 lakh over four years, meaning the grant must clear that plus the risk to be worth it. Then the cash questions: exercising the full grant costs ₹6,00,000, and perquisite tax at exercise would be substantial at current valuations, all payable with no buyer in sight. The 90-day window means that if she leaves in year three, she must fund both within three months. What to ask: the latest merchant banker valuation and its date, since that is what her tax would be based on rather than the round price; the preference terms on the ₹900 crore; whether the company holds an Inter-Ministerial Board certificate, which would let her defer perquisite tax; whether a buyback is planned and what the board has actually discussed; and whether the exercise window can be extended, which is the term most worth negotiating. My advice: treat the ₹72 lakh as a lottery ticket with a real cost, negotiate the window hard, take the job if the work and the cash are right on their own, and never let the ESOP alone justify an ₹8 lakh annual pay cut.

children.text: The Questions This Course Has Given You

body.title: Ask These About Any Grant, for the Rest of Your Career
steps: What instrument is this: ESOP, RSU, SAR, ESPS, sweat equity or phantom stock?
How many options, at what exercise price, against how many fully diluted shares?
What percentage of the company is that?
What is the vesting schedule, and when exactly is the cliff?
How long is the exercise window if I leave?
How much capital have investors put in, and on what liquidity preference terms?
What is the latest fair market value, from what date, and who certified it?
What will I owe in perquisite tax when I exercise, and can I fund it?
Is the company an eligible startup, so that tax can be deferred?
What liquidity events has this company run, in which years?
What cash salary am I giving up, and what share value do I need to beat it?
If this grant went to zero, would I still be glad I took this job?

children.text: That last question is the one that matters most. Every employee in the winning cases above would have answered yes. Many in the cautionary ones would not have.

points: Outcomes were decided by liquidity, not by grant size.
Infosys showed what breadth plus a real market can do; Flipkart showed what a repeated liquidity track record looks like.
Swiggy’s listing created a price for thousands of employees, but a listing is a market, not a guaranteed gain.
Paytm fell roughly 78% from its issue price, leaving options with high exercise prices underwater despite being listed.
Byju’s showed that a headline valuation you cannot sell into is not wealth.
Exercising at a peak and watching the price fall is the most expensive mistake available: the perquisite tax is not refunded, and the loss is a capital loss.
Ask for a company’s liquidity history before you join. It is public, and it predicts your outcome better than any valuation headline.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment, tax or legal advice. All company facts are as publicly reported and may be revised; nothing here is a comment on the conduct of any company or individual, and no example is a recommendation to buy or sell any security. Tax figures assume a 30% slab with 4% cess and ignore surcharge.
